# Visualisation and gene set enrichment {#sec-viz}

A results table with 20,000 rows is hard to read. Plots help, but each plot
type has rules that keep it honest. In this chapter we draw an MA plot, a
volcano plot and a heatmap, and then ask whether whole pathways shift with
gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA).

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/helpers.R")
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(DESeq2)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(ggrepel)
  library(pheatmap)
  library(dplyr)
  library(fgsea)
  library(msigdbr)
})
f_dds <- cache_path("dds_TDP43_vs_scramble.rds")
if (!file.exists(f_dds)) stop("Run the differential expression chapter first.")
dds <- readRDS(f_dds)
de  <- read.csv("results/de_deseq2_TDP43_vs_scramble.csv")
de$DE <- factor(de$DE, levels = c("down", "not significant", "up"))
DE_COLS <- c(down = "#0072B2", `not significant` = "grey75", up = "#D55E00")
```

## MA plot

An MA plot shows the fold change (M) against mean expression (A). It is the
best plot to see whether the fold changes behave sensibly across the
expression range.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ma
#| fig-cap: "MA plot. Each point is a gene; the y-axis is the apeglm-shrunken log2 fold change (TDP-43 knockdown vs scramble). Dashed lines mark |log2FC| = 1."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(arrange(de, DE != "not significant"), aes(log10(baseMean), log2FC_shrunk, colour = DE)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-DE_LFC, DE_LFC), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = DE_COLS) +
  labs(x = "log10 mean of normalised counts", y = "log2 fold change (shrunken)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_tutorial()
```

The cloud is centred on zero across the expression range, which is what we
expect when most genes do not change and normalisation worked. Shrinkage
limits how far low-count genes on the left can fan out, so the genes that
still cross the dashed lines there have consistent evidence across samples.
Notice, though, that most of the genes called "up" are lowly expressed
(mean normalised count below about 100). Look at their counts sample by
sample before building a biological story on any one of them.

## Volcano plot

A volcano plot shows effect size against evidence. Two rules:

1. **Use padj, not the raw p-value**, both for the y-axis and for the colour.
   Colouring by raw p < 0.05 would highlight hundreds of genes that do not
   survive multiple-testing correction.
2. **Choose labels by a rule, not by hand.** We label the 10 most significant
   genes, the 5 largest fold changes among significant genes, and a panel of
   genes defined before the analysis (*TARDBP*, the knockdown target, and
   three literature examples, *STMN2*, *UNC13A*, *POLDIP3*).

```{r}
#| label: labels
panel <- c("TARDBP", "STMN2", "UNC13A", "POLDIP3")
sig <- filter(de, DE != "not significant")
lab_rule <- union(slice_min(sig, padj, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE)$gene_id,
                  slice_max(sig, abs(log2FC_shrunk), n = 5, with_ties = FALSE)$gene_id)
de <- de |>
  mutate(label = case_when(symbol %in% panel ~ symbol,
                           gene_id %in% lab_rule ~ symbol,
                           TRUE ~ NA_character_),
         label_type = ifelse(symbol %in% panel, "panel", "rule"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-volcano
#| fig-cap: "Volcano plot. y-axis: -log10 adjusted p-value (Benjamini-Hochberg). Dashed lines: padj = 0.05 and |log2FC| = 1. Bold labels: predefined gene panel; plain labels: 10 smallest padj and 5 largest |log2FC| among significant genes."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
ymax <- -log10(min(de$padj[de$padj > 0], na.rm = TRUE))
de_plot <- de |>
  filter(!is.na(padj)) |>
  mutate(y = pmin(-log10(padj), ymax)) |>
  arrange(DE != "not significant")
ggplot(de_plot, aes(log2FC_shrunk, y, colour = DE)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.9, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(DE_PADJ), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-DE_LFC, DE_LFC), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(de_plot, !is.na(label)),
                  aes(label = label, fontface = ifelse(label_type == "panel", "bold", "plain")),
                  colour = "black", size = 3, max.overlaps = Inf, min.segment.length = 0,
                  seed = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = DE_COLS) +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change (shrunken)", y = expression(-log[10]~"adjusted p-value"), colour = NULL) +
  theme_tutorial()
```

Many genes sit above the padj line but between the fold change lines: they
change significantly but by less than two-fold. Whether those matter
biologically is a question the thresholds cannot answer for you; what
matters is that the thresholds were fixed beforehand and are reported.

## Heatmap

Heatmaps should never be drawn from raw counts: library size and the
mean-variance relationship would dominate the colours. We use
variance-stabilised values and scale each row to a z-score, so the colour
shows how a sample compares with the average of that gene.

Because batch is the largest source of variation (@sec-qc), we remove it
from the values **for display only**, exactly as in the QC chapter.

```{r}
#| label: fig-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Top 40 differentially expressed genes (smallest padj). VST values with the batch effect removed for display, scaled to row z-scores."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 8
vsd <- vst(dds, blind = FALSE)
mat <- limma::removeBatchEffect(assay(vsd), batch = vsd$batch,
                                design = model.matrix(~ condition, colData(vsd)))
top <- sig |> slice_min(padj, n = 40, with_ties = FALSE)
z <- t(scale(t(mat[top$gene_id, ])))
rownames(z) <- top$symbol
ann <- data.frame(condition = vsd$condition, batch = vsd$batch, row.names = colnames(vsd))
pheatmap(z, annotation_col = ann, show_colnames = FALSE,
         annotation_colors = list(condition = SIRNA_COLS[c("scramble", "TDP43")],
                                  batch = c(B1 = "grey30", B2 = "grey80")),
         color = colorRampPalette(c("#0072B2", "white", "#D55E00"))(101),
         breaks = seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = 102), fontsize_row = 8)
```

The columns separate cleanly into knockdown and control, which is expected:
we selected these genes *because* they differ between the groups. A heatmap
of top DE genes illustrates the result; it is not independent evidence for
it.

## Gene set enrichment analysis

Single-gene thresholds throw away information: a pathway in which 80 genes
each go up by 20% can matter more than one gene that goes up 4-fold. GSEA
[@subramanian2005] ranks **all** tested genes and asks whether the members
of a gene set are concentrated near the top or the bottom of the ranking.
We use the fast implementation in fgsea [@korotkevich2019] and the 50
MSigDB Hallmark gene sets [@liberzon2015], which were designed to be
concise and non-redundant.

### The ranking metric

The ranking metric must be stated, because the results depend on it. We use
the **DESeq2 Wald statistic** (`stat`), which combines effect size and its
precision: genes with large, well-measured changes rank at the extremes,
while noisy genes stay near the middle. The shrunken log2 fold change is a
reasonable alternative; raw p-values are not, because they lose the
direction.

```{r}
#| label: ranks
de$ensembl <- sub("\\..*$", "", de$gene_id)   # drop the GENCODE version suffix
ranks <- de |>
  filter(!is.na(stat), !grepl("_PAR_Y", gene_id)) |>
  group_by(ensembl) |>
  slice_max(abs(stat), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()
ranks <- setNames(ranks$stat, ranks$ensembl)
length(ranks)
```

### Hallmark gene sets

The msigdbr package bundles MSigDB in R. We match genes by Ensembl ID
rather than by symbol, because symbols change between annotation releases
more often than IDs.

```{r}
#| label: hallmark
hallmark <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", category = "H")
pathways <- split(hallmark$human_ensembl_gene, hallmark$gs_name)
c(msigdbr_version = as.character(packageVersion("msigdbr")),
  hallmark_sets = length(pathways),
  hallmark_genes = length(unique(hallmark$human_ensembl_gene)),
  matched_in_ranking = sum(unique(hallmark$human_ensembl_gene) %in% names(ranks)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fgsea
set.seed(42)
gsea <- fgsea(pathways, ranks, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500, eps = 0)
gsea <- gsea |> arrange(padj)
gsea |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(padj < 0.05) |>
  transmute(pathway = sub("HALLMARK_", "", pathway), size, NES = round(NES, 2),
            padj = formatC(padj, format = "e", digits = 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gsea-bar
#| fig-cap: "Hallmark gene sets with padj < 0.05. Normalised enrichment score (NES) > 0: genes of the set tend to be higher in the knockdown; NES < 0: lower. Ranking metric: DESeq2 Wald statistic."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
gsea |>
  filter(padj < 0.05) |>
  mutate(pathway = reorder(sub("HALLMARK_", "", pathway), NES)) |>
  ggplot(aes(NES, pathway, fill = NES > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#D55E00", `FALSE` = "#0072B2"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Normalised enrichment score", y = NULL) +
  theme_tutorial()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gsea-curve
#| fig-cap: "Running enrichment score for the most significant Hallmark set. Ticks show where the members of the set fall in the ranking (left: higher in knockdown)."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
top_set <- gsea$pathway[1]
plotEnrichment(pathways[[top_set]], ranks) +
  labs(title = sub("HALLMARK_", "", top_set), x = "Rank (Wald statistic, high to low)") +
  theme_tutorial()
```

```{r}
#| label: save-gsea
gsea_out <- gsea |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(leadingEdge = vapply(leadingEdge, paste, character(1), collapse = ";"),
         ranking_metric = "DESeq2 Wald statistic (stat)")
write.csv(gsea_out, "results/gsea_hallmark_TDP43_vs_scramble.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

### What the result says, and what it does not

The strongest sets are proliferation signatures (E2F targets, G2M
checkpoint) and interferon responses, all shifted towards higher expression
in the knockdown. Two cautious readings:

- **Proliferation sets** in a culture of post-mitotic neurons most likely
  reflect how many dividing cells (progenitors or non-neuronal cells) the
  culture contains, not something that happens inside neurons. Bulk RNA-seq
  of a mixed culture cannot separate a change in cell composition from a
  change in gene regulation.
- **Interferon sets** suggest an innate immune-like response. The scramble
  control also received an siRNA, so a generic transfection effect is
  unlikely to explain it fully, but an effect specific to this particular
  siRNA sequence cannot be excluded with a single targeting siRNA. A second,
  independent siRNA (or a rescue experiment) is the experimental answer.

Both are hypotheses generated by the data, not findings about TDP-43
biology.

### How to interpret GSEA results in general

- A significant gene set says that **its members are shifted as a group** in
  the ranking. It does not say that the pathway is "activated": many
  Hallmark sets mix genes with opposite roles, and mRNA level is not
  activity.
- Look at the **leading edge** (saved in the results table): the subset of
  genes that drives the score. Two sets that share their leading edge are
  one finding, not two.
- Hallmark sets were mostly derived from other cell types. A set such as
  "epithelial-mesenchymal transition" in motor neuron cultures may reflect
  extracellular matrix genes in the non-neuronal cells of the culture
  rather than a change of cell identity.
- To test your own hypothesis (for example a set of calcium signalling
  genes), define the set **before** looking at the results, add it to the
  `pathways` list, and report it separately from the genome-wide Hallmark
  analysis.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding
1. Why would a volcano plot coloured by raw p < 0.05 be misleading here?
2. A reviewer asks why *GENE_X* is labelled in your volcano plot. What is a
   good answer?
3. The heatmap of the top 40 genes separates the two groups perfectly. Is
   that evidence that the knockdown has a strong effect?
4. Why do we rank by the Wald statistic rather than by p-value?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers
1. With 20,000 tests, about 1,000 genes would have p < 0.05 by chance alone.
   Only padj accounts for multiple testing.
2. "Labels were assigned by a predefined rule: the 10 smallest padj, the 5
   largest |log2FC| among significant genes, and a panel defined before the
   analysis." Hand-picked labels invite the suspicion of selective
   reporting.
3. No. The genes were selected because they differ between the groups, so
   perfect separation is guaranteed to some degree. The PCA in @sec-qc, which
   does not use the labels, is the fairer view.
4. A p-value has no sign, so up- and down-regulated genes would be mixed at
   the top of the ranking. The Wald statistic keeps the direction and
   weights each change by its precision.
:::
:::
